steps.text: Part 2 of 3: Opposition: one tempo between a win and a draw. This part covers Set it up or prevent it; Near misses. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Setting it up.** You take the opposition by stepping onto the facing square, so before moving ask three things. Am I one step from that square? Whose move is it afterwards? Does my pawn have a spare step that changes the answer? A pawn on its second or third rank has such steps.
steps.chapter: Set it up or prevent it

steps.caption: White to move. The only winning move is the step to the facing square. The pawn push only draws.

line.say: The king steps to the facing square: one square between the kings, Black to move.
Black must give way.
White's king moves forward past the pawn's file.
Black steps in front.
White's king goes beside the black king.
Black steps aside.

claims.statement: With White to move the tablebase result for White is a win.

steps.caption: White to move. Two king moves win. One faces the black king; the other, toward the d-file, also wins because White can take the opposition one move later (distant opposition, explained below). Both pawn pushes and the sideways king steps only draw.

line.say: The king steps to the facing square: one square between the kings, Black to move.
Black gives way.
White's king goes forward on the other side.
Black steps down beside the pawn's file.
Now the pawn takes a spare step; the king guards it.
Black retreats.
White's king keeps its lead.
Black has run out of room.

claims.statement: With White to move the tablebase result for White is a win.
The two-square pawn step only draws.

steps.caption: The kings already face, but it is White's move. Reaching the facing square at the wrong moment is not enough: this is a draw.

line.say: White steps aside to get round.
Black copies at once, and the kings face again with White to move.
White tries the other side.
Black copies again.

claims.statement: With White to move the tablebase result for White is a draw.

steps.caption: White to move. A pawn on its third rank has a spare step. Spending it hands the move to Black while the kings still face.

line.say: The spare step: the kings face and Black must move.
Black gives way.
White's king steps forward to the sixth rank.
Black falls back.
White keeps pace.
Black swings round.
The pawn moves on.

claims.statement: With White to move the tablebase result for White is a win.

steps.text: **Distant opposition.** Kings can also face each other from farther away: on one file or rank with an odd number of empty squares between them, such as three. [I] The same parity rule applies, checked board by board: the side not to move holds it, and a later step can turn it into the close opposition. A diagonal works in the same way. On the next board, White reaches the same file as Black's king with three empty squares between.

steps.title: Same pieces, other player to move
steps.prompt: Original first: Black to move, and White wins. Now White is to move instead. Predict the result, then check. The third position moves everything one file to the left, with Black to move.

steps.caption: White to move. The king steps to the d-file with three empty squares between the kings and Black to move: the distant opposition. Kc4 also wins here; the pawn push and every other king move only draw.

line.say: The distant opposition: same file, three squares between, Black to move.
Black gives way.
White's king steps forward.
Black returns to the file.
White's king slips past to the sixth rank.
Black has run out of useful squares.

claims.statement: With White to move the tablebase result for White is a win.

steps.caption: The same placement with Black to move: a draw. [I] After Kd7, White can no longer reach a file with an odd number of squares between the kings and Black to move.

line.say: Black steps to the file where White cannot take the distant opposition.
White comes forward.
Black now holds the close opposition.
The pawn moves on.
Black stays in front of the pawn: a draw.

claims.statement: With Black to move the tablebase result for Black is a draw.

steps.title: Same pawn, wrong king square
steps.prompt: Original again. In the second position White's king stands on d5, level with the pawn. In the third the pawn is on e3 and the kings are as in the original.

steps.text: **A third kind of failure: the edge of the board.** A pawn on the a-file or h-file leaves the attacker only one side to go round. If the defending king reaches the corner, the attacker must avoid **stalemate**: a position where the side to move has no legal move and is not in check, which is a draw. [I] If the defender is too far away, the pawn still queens. The tablebase boards below are the proof.

steps.title: Edge file or not?
steps.prompt: Original first: a b-pawn, White's king in front, Black to move, and White wins. In the second position the pawn is on the a-file. In the third everything has moved one file to the right.

steps.caption: First the normal case. The pawn is on the g-file, one file in from the edge, and Black to move loses.

line.say: Black has one legal move.
White's king steps aside to the sixth rank beside the pawn's path.
Black comes out of the corner.
The pawn steps ahead with check, guarded by the king.
Black attacks the pawn, but the king guards it.

claims.statement: With Black to move the tablebase result for Black is a loss.

steps.caption: Black to move. This is the h-pawn. The same king placing with the g-pawn wins, but here Black draws.

line.say: Black has one legal move.
White pushes, but Black's king stays near the corner.
Black steps back into the corner.
White makes a waiting move, but no progress follows.
Black shuffles between the corner squares.
White tries again.
Black shuffles again, and the draw stands.

claims.statement: With Black to move the tablebase result for Black is a draw.

steps.caption: The edge-file trap in its purest form. Black has no legal move and is not in check: stalemate, so the game is drawn.

claims.statement: Black is stalemated: no legal move, not in check.

steps.caption: A fourth case: the defender is too far away. Black's king never reaches the pawn's path, and White wins with either side to move, so the opposition never comes up.

line.say: Black heads towards the pawn.
White's king steps up beside its pawn.
Black comes closer.
White's king guards the pawn from the front.
Black circles.
White's king moves ahead, and Black's king is still too far from the pawn.

claims.statement: With Black to move the tablebase result for Black is a loss.

steps.text: **A reversal on the sixth rank.** Edward Lasker's notes mark the moment the pawn reaches its sixth rank as critical [S]. With the black king on e8 and the white king beside the pawn, White to move wins and Black to move draws. [I] That reverses the usual rule, but not for every layout: with the black king on d8, White wins whoever moves. Predict on the next board.

steps.caption: White to move. The king stands beside the pawn on the sixth rank. The pawn push wins; every king step only draws.

line.say: The pawn steps ahead, guarded by its king, and Black's king has no good square.
Black attacks the pawn.
White's king takes the squares in front and guards the pawn.
Black's king still cannot touch the pawn.
The pawn becomes a queen.

claims.statement: With White to move the tablebase result for White is a win.

steps.caption: The same placement with Black to move: a draw. Black must keep the king beside the pawn's file.

line.say: The only drawing move: the king stays beside the pawn's file.
The pawn gives check.
Black must step in front of the pawn.
White's king steps to e6 and Black is stalemated, so it is a draw.

claims.statement: With Black to move the tablebase result for Black is a draw.

steps.caption: The last position of that line: Black has no legal move and is not in check. Stalemate, and the game is drawn.

claims.statement: Black is stalemated: no legal move, not in check.

steps.text: **Remember.** Take the opposition by stepping onto the facing square, so the other side must move. Before moving, ask: am I one step from that square, and whose move is it afterwards? A pawn's spare step can change the answer. It fails with an edge-file pawn, where the corner and stalemate give a draw, and it never comes up when the defender is too far away.
